entities.name: Hittite Empire
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Hittite Empire (c. 1650–1178 BCE), centered on Hattusa in modern Anatolia (central Turkey), was the first Iron Age superpower of the ancient Near East — the earliest known user of iron weapons, the author of the world's oldest known peace treaty (with Egypt, 1259 BCE), and the civilization that fought Egypt's Ramesses II to a stalemate at the Battle of Kadesh (1274 BCE), the largest chariot battle in history. The Hittites' sudden collapse during the Late Bronze Age Crisis (c. 1200 BCE) — along with Egypt, Mycenae, and the Ugarit trading city — remains one of history's most debated civilizational collapses.

The Hittites spoke the earliest attested member of the Indo-European language family (confirmed in 1915 by Czech linguist Bedřich Hrozný's decipherment), proving that Indo-European languages originated in or near Anatolia. Their capital Hattusa, discovered in 1906 and excavated since, revealed a complex administrative state with 30,000+ clay tablets in the Hittite archive — including the Mitanni treaty, law codes, and religious texts. The Hittite pantheon of 1,000 gods was the most complex in the Bronze Age.

The Battle of Kadesh (1274 BCE) — fought between Ramesses II and Muwatalli II over Syria — involved 5,000-6,000 chariots on each side. Neither side won decisively, but both claimed victory. The subsequent Treaty of Kadesh (1259 BCE) — concluded between Ramesses and Hattusili III — is the world's oldest surviving peace treaty, with copies in both Egyptian hieroglyphs and Hittite cuneiform. A reproduction hangs in the United Nations headquarters. The empire's collapse c. 1178 BCE — burned and abandoned — remains unexplained (drought, Sea Peoples invasion, internal collapse, or all three).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Hittite Empire's Treaty of Kadesh — the world's oldest surviving peace treaty, now reproduced in the United Nations — and its earliest attested Indo-European language make it the Bronze Age civilization with the most enduring contributions to international law and linguistic science.
